*Interview with Bastien Girard, établisseur, of Le Locle, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Monsieur Girard. You have spoken to the constable already, and I have read his note. I shall ask you some things again, and you may tell me if I have them wrong.

GIRARD: Ask, then. It is cold in here. Nobody has seen to the fire.

MATTHEY: Tell me about dinner.

GIRARD: Dinner was good. The master was in good spirits, which means he was enjoying himself at other people's expense. He always has the watches brought out on the table as though we were schoolboys, and then he tells each man what is wrong with his.

MATTHEY: Did he tell you what was wrong with yours?

GIRARD: I would not show him mine. I said so across the table, and he laughed and said I was afraid of his opinion. I said I was afraid of nothing but a bad price.

MATTHEY: A bad price?

GIRARD: For the repeater. I offered to take up the rights to it and make it under my firm's name, in proper numbers. That is a fair offer for a watch nobody else has seen. He wanted more than I can pay and more than it is worth. We said things to each other. I will not pretend otherwise. I told him he was an old man asking a good price for a thing he will not let anyone else finish. I would say it again.

MATTHEY: And Félix Monnier?

GIRARD: Félix owes me money. A good deal of it, and he has not paid, and he has been very amusing about it. I do not think he is a bad boy. I think he is a frightened one who makes jokes, and I have never seen a joke pay a debt.

MATTHEY: What did you do after dinner?

GIRARD: I sat on alone in the dining room with the brandy. I heard the temple strike ten there. I did not look at my watch.

MATTHEY: Go on.

GIRARD: I went out into the street to smoke, at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, and I stayed under the front windows of the house. I smoke Brissago cigars, Inspector, the cheap ones. A merchant has no business with a good cigar when the buyer is waiting. It was cold. I walk in the cold when I want to think, and I wanted to think.

MATTHEY: What did you hear while you stood there?

GIRARD: The piano started up in the salon just as I lit my cigar, at twenty-nine minutes past ten by my watch. I do not know music. I know the sound of a piano being played, and that is all I know of it.

MATTHEY: Anything else?

GIRARD: At twenty-six minutes to eleven by my watch I heard faint quick bells from the master's window up above.

MATTHEY: What kind of bells?

GIRARD: I will not say what they were. I heard faint, quick bells from his window. I will swear to that and nothing more. A man who sells watches does not describe sounds he cannot see.

MATTHEY: Then what did you do?

GIRARD: I came back into the house at fourteen minutes to eleven by my watch. The hall clock had just struck eleven, and its face showed two minutes past eleven. I went straight up to Félix in the library.

MATTHEY: Why did you go to him?

GIRARD: Because he was in the library, and because he owes me money, and I wanted an answer about it. You may look at the hall clock yourself. It is the old Morbier by the stairs. It shows what it shows.

MATTHEY: Thank you. Is there anything you have not told me that you think I should know?

GIRARD: Only that a merchant notices the time, Inspector. It is what he is paid for. I have given you every hour I am sure of, and I am sure of those.
